input:
The appraisal of the bottling line returns a net present value of $156k, which indicates that, on the basis of the estimates that have been stated, the line is worth installing. It should be emphasised, however, that the finding rests on vendor and utility estimates throughout, and that the associated limit must be borne in mind: no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.

The installed cost amounts to $838k. The expected net saving is $160k per year over a period of 8 years, discounted at a rate of 6%. On this basis, the present value of the savings is calculated to be $994k. The net present value is obtained as the difference between that present value and the installed cost, namely $994k less $838k, which gives $156k.

The result is positive at the stated discount rate, although the margin is relatively thin when it is considered in relation to the size of the two figures from which it is derived: the net present value is the difference between two estimates of comparable size, so that a modest shortfall in the saving, or a modest overrun in the installed cost, would be sufficient to remove it entirely. The saving estimate represents the weak element of the appraisal. It combines vendor figures for the line itself with utility estimates, and neither of these has been tested on a comparable installation at this site.

The next step is therefore to obtain a check on the saving before the order is placed: either a measured saving from a comparable line, or a vendor guarantee that would convert the estimate into a firm commitment. The installed cost can be firmed up by means of a quotation, but the saving cannot, and the appraisal should accordingly be re-run with the checked figure before the capital is committed.

The discount rate is not the contested figure: at any plausible rate, the difference of the two estimates stays of the same order, and the decision does not turn on the choice of rate. That check, and not a refinement of the arithmetic, is what the appraisal lacks.
